meta.subject: maths
meta.title: Pair of Linear Equations in Two Variables
meta.source_edition: NCERT Reprint 2026-27, Class 10 Mathematics, Ch 3 (jemh103.pdf, printed pages 24–37)

board_asks: solving a pair by substitution and by elimination, reading a solution off a graph, and classifying a pair as consistent / inconsistent / dependent from the coefficient ratios — the two algebraic methods plus a word-problem application carry almost every mark here.

big_idea.body: A pair of linear equations in two variables is two straight-line equations $a_1x + b_1y + c_1 = 0$ and $a_2x + b_2y + c_2 = 0$ that you solve together. Geometrically each is a line, so the whole chapter answers one question: where do the two lines meet? They can cross once (one solution), run parallel (no solution), or lie on top of each other (infinitely many). You learn to find that meeting point three ways — by graph, by substitution, and by elimination — and to predict the outcome just from the coefficient ratios.

definitions.verbatim: A pair of linear equations in two variables, which has a solution, is called a consistent pair of linear equations.
definitions.plain: any pair that HAS at least one solution — the lines either cross once (unique) or coincide (infinitely many). “Has a solution” is the whole test.

definitions.verbatim: A pair of linear equations which has no solution, is called an inconsistent pair of linear equations.
definitions.plain: the lines are parallel and never meet, so there is NO common $(x,y)$. In working, a false statement like $0 = 9$ signals this.

definitions.verbatim: A pair of linear equations which are equivalent has infinitely many distinct common solutions. Such a pair is called a dependent pair of linear equations in two variables. Note that a dependent pair of linear equations is always consistent.
definitions.plain: the two equations are really the SAME line (coincident), so every point on it solves both — infinitely many solutions. A dependent pair is a special case of consistent, never inconsistent.

definitions.verbatim: We have substituted the value of one variable by expressing it in terms of the other variable to solve the pair of linear equations. That is why the method is known as the substitution method.
definitions.plain: isolate one variable in one equation ($x = \dots$), then substitute it into the other so only one variable is left. Fastest when a coefficient is already $1$.

source.note: the substitution-method Remark that closes Section 3.3.1

definitions.verbatim: The method used in solving the example above is called the elimination method, because we eliminate one variable first, to get a linear equation in one variable.
definitions.plain: multiply the equations so one variable’s coefficients match, then add or subtract to cancel that variable. Best when neither variable is already isolated.

definitions.verbatim: The graph of a pair of linear equations in two variables is represented by two lines.
Algebraic Methods : We have discussed the following methods for finding the solution(s) of a pair of linear equations : (i) Substitution Method (ii) Elimination Method

source.note: Summary point 3 — the only two algebraic methods in the rationalised 2026-27 chapter

definitions.verbatim: There are several situations which can be mathematically represented by two equations that are not linear to start with. But we alter them so that they are reduced to a pair of linear equations.

concepts.title: Graphical method — three cases
concepts.body: Plot both lines. They either intersect at one point (unique solution, consistent), coincide (infinitely many, dependent), or are parallel (no solution, inconsistent). The meeting point read off the graph IS the solution.
concepts.tested: Graphically solve / find the triangle formed with an axis — 3 marks

concepts.title: Classify from the coefficient ratios
concepts.body: For $a_1x+b_1y+c_1=0$ and $a_2x+b_2y+c_2=0$: $\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}\neq\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}$ → intersecting (one solution) · $\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}=\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}\neq\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}$ → parallel (none) · $\dfrac{a_1}{a_2}=\dfrac{b_1}{b_2}=\dfrac{c_1}{c_2}$ → coincident (infinitely many). Compare the ratios best on a diagram:
concepts.tested: “Without solving, state whether the pair is consistent” — 1–2 marks

concepts.title: Substitution method
concepts.body: Express one variable from one equation ($x = 3 - 2y$), substitute into the other to get a single-variable equation, solve it, then back-substitute for the second variable. A no-variable TRUE statement means infinitely many solutions; a FALSE one means no solution.

concepts.title: Elimination method
concepts.body: Multiply the two equations by suitable non-zero constants to make one variable’s coefficients numerically equal, then add or subtract to eliminate it. Solve the resulting one-variable equation and back-substitute. Often quicker than substitution when nothing is pre-isolated.
concepts.tested: “Solve by elimination” / solve by BOTH methods — 2–3 marks

concepts.title: Word problems → a pair of equations
concepts.body: Translate the situation (ages, digits, fractions, incomes, fixed-plus-variable charges) into TWO equations in two unknowns, solve by substitution or elimination, and check the answer against the story. Some non-linear situations are first reduced to a linear pair before solving.
concepts.tested: Applied problem — a fixture of Sections C/D, 3–5 marks

examples.problem_verbatim: Check graphically whether the pair of equations x + 3y = 6 and 2x – 3y = 12 is consistent. If so, solve them graphically.

solution_steps.text: The lines meet at $B(6,0)$, so $x=6,\;y=0$; the given pair is consistent.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark graphical shape: 1 for a correct table of two solutions per line, 1 for plotting both lines accurately, 1 for reading the common point $(6,0)$ and stating the pair is consistent.

source.note: problem stated on p.26; solution table (Table 3.2) and graph (Fig. 3.1) on p.27

examples.problem_verbatim: Solve the following pair of equations by substitution method: 7x – 15y = 2 x + 2y = 3

solution_steps.concept_tag: express x in terms of y

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark substitution: 1 for expressing one variable in terms of the other, 1 for substituting and solving for $y$, 1 for back-substituting to get $x$ and stating both values. NCERT verifies both equations are satisfied.

examples.problem_verbatim: The ratio of incomes of two persons is 9 : 7 and the ratio of their expenditures is 4 : 3. If each of them manages to save ₹ 2000 per month, find their monthly incomes.

solution_steps.lead: Model the ratios into two equations.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark elimination: 1 for forming the pair from the ratios, 1 for making the $y$-coefficients equal and eliminating to get $x$, 1 for back-substituting for $y$ and reporting the two incomes ₹18,000 and ₹14,000.

examples.problem_verbatim: The sum of a two-digit number and the number obtained by reversing the digits is 66. If the digits of the number differ by 2, find the number. How many such numbers are there?

solution_steps.text: Ten’s digit $x$, unit’s digit $y$: the number is $10x+y$ and the reversed number is $10y+x$.
Sum is $66$: $(10x+y)+(10y+x)=66\Rightarrow 11(x+y)=66\Rightarrow x+y=6$. Digits differ by $2$: $x-y=2$ or $y-x=2$.

solution_steps.lead: Solve each case; state BOTH numbers.
solution_steps.text: $x+y=6$ with $x-y=2\Rightarrow(4,2)\to 42$; with $y-x=2\Rightarrow(2,4)\to 24$. So there are two such numbers: 42 and 24.

examples.mark_logic: 3-mark word problem: 1 for expressing the number as $10x+y$ and forming $x+y=6$, 1 for setting up both difference conditions, 1 for solving each case by elimination and stating both numbers 42 and 24. Reporting only one number is the classic lost mark — NCERT verifies both.

source.note: problem on p.35, solution runs to p.36

strategies.text: Use substitution — write that variable in terms of the other and plug it in.
Use elimination — scale to match one variable’s coefficients, then add or subtract.

strategies.cue: Graph would give ugly / non-integer coordinates?
strategies.text: Switch to an algebraic method — NCERT’s own reason for introducing them (p.30).

strategies.cue: Hit a statement with no variable?
strategies.text: TRUE (e.g. $18=18$) ⇒ infinitely many solutions; FALSE (e.g. $0=9$) ⇒ no solution.
Name two variables → form two equations → solve → verify against the story.

pitfalls.text: Misreading a graphical intersection — non-integer coordinates are easy to read wrong; if the crossing isn’t on clean grid points, solve algebraically instead.
Swapping the no-solution / infinite-solution verdict — a TRUE no-variable line ($18=18$) means infinitely many; a FALSE one ($0=9$) means no solution. Students reverse these.
Eliminating without matching coefficients — you must first scale so one variable’s coefficients are numerically equal (and mind the sign: add if opposite, subtract if same).
Confusing the ratio conditions — parallel/inconsistent is $\tfrac{a_1}{a_2}=\tfrac{b_1}{b_2}\neq\tfrac{c_1}{c_2}$; coincident/dependent needs ALL three ratios equal.
Stopping at one answer in a two-case word problem — e.g. the two-digit number gives 42 AND 24; report every valid solution.

third_tab_content.name: Why the coefficient ratios decide the fate of a pair
third_tab_content.intro: NCERT establishes the ratio conditions inductively — it tabulates three sample pairs (Table 3.1, p.26), reads off $\tfrac{a_1}{a_2},\tfrac{b_1}{b_2},\tfrac{c_1}{c_2}$ for each, and states that “the converse is also true for any pair of lines.” Here is the slope reasoning behind that table, so the three ratio rules are understood rather than memorised. The conditions themselves are exactly NCERT’s (Table 3.1 and Summary point 4).

steps.claim: Write the pair in general form — each equation is a straight line.
Rearranged to slope–intercept form, a line has slope $-a/b$ and $y$-intercept $-c/b$ (for $b\neq 0$).
steps.justification: Two lines cross exactly once iff their slopes differ, are parallel iff slopes match but intercepts differ, and are the same line iff both match.

steps.claim: Different slopes ⇒ the lines intersect at one point ⇒ a unique solution (consistent).
steps.justification: NCERT: intersecting lines give exactly one solution (Table 3.1, p.26; Summary 4(i), p.37).

steps.claim: Equal slopes but different intercepts ⇒ parallel lines that never meet ⇒ no solution (inconsistent).
steps.justification: No common point, so the pair has no solution (p.26; Summary 4(ii), p.37).

steps.claim: All three ratios equal ⇒ the two equations describe the SAME line ⇒ infinitely many solutions (dependent, hence consistent).
steps.justification: Every point of the line satisfies both equations (p.26; Summary 4(iii), p.37).

source.note: conditions stated in Table 3.1 and the paragraph after it (p.26) and again as Summary point 4 (p.37); the slope reasoning is the standard justification, which NCERT presents inductively across three worked pairs.
